newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul analysts sceptical over Ssangyong-GM link-up.
newsitem.headline: Seoul analysts sceptical over Ssangyong-GM link-up.

text.p: South Korea's Ssangyong Group said on Thursday it was talking to General Motors Corp and other foreign companies about investing $300 million in its struggling automaker.
The news sent shares in key affiliates of the country's sixth-largest conglomerate skyrocketing, but analysts were sceptical that a deal would be reached soon.
"What GM wants is to sell more of its cars in Korea and I doubt it is interested in linking up with Ssangyong to give help," said Hur Kang, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
The president of General Motors-Korea told Reuters that discussions between General Motors and Ssangyong Motor Co were nowhere near the point of public comment.
Alan Perriton also said that GM had concluded no agreement with Ssangyong and he did not understand why Ssangyong would be making public statements at this stage.

"We've had discussions with Ssangyong, but they haven't proceeded to any level where we would be making confirmations or issuing statements," Perriton said. "Ssangyong is just one of the South Korean car companies we're having discussions with."
Analysts said Ssangyong's comments could be viewed as a move to boost share prices of its affiliates.

"I think these guys are probably trying to draw attention to their shares and encourage lenders to view them in a favourable light," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K) Ltd, a securities firm.
Ssangyong Motor, Ssangyong Precision Industry Co and Ssangyong Heavy Industries Co bucked the weakness on the Seoul bourse on Thursday and rose by their daily limits.
Ssangyong Motor was up 420 won to 5,740, Ssangyong Precision up 380 won to 5,130, and Ssangyong Heavy up 380 won to 5,130.
Earlier on Thursday, Cho Nam-do, a vice president of the Ssangyong Group, said discussions were underway with GM and other foreign companies about the capital investment.
He said the other foreign companies included several Southeast Asian companies owned and run by ethnic Chinese.
Analysts said a partnership with Asian companies would help Ssangyong, which specialises in making four-wheel-drive utility vehicles and trucks, sharply expand sales.
"Roads are still underdeveloped in many Asian nations and demand for utility vehicles is relatively high there," said Hur of Hyundai.
Mercedes-Benz, a unit of Germany's Daimler-Benz AG, held a 2.6-percent stake in Ssangyong Motor as of the end of 1996, while the Ssangyong Group has a 40.2-percent stake.
Ssangyong Motor saw its net loss widen to 228.5 billion won ($256.7 million) in calendar 1996 from the previous year's 126.2-billion-won loss.
In March, Ssangyong Motor invited foreigners to purchase up to 49 percent of the company in a desperate effort to ease the burden of its snowballing debt.

Later it said it would sell its headquarters building and other real estate and assets to raise cash to pay back debt, estimated at 3.73 trillion won at the end of 1996, against 35.54 billion won of shareholders' equity.
Cho said a fresh injection of $300 million would help reduce the company's debt-equity ratio to around 1,000 percent from over 10,000 percent at the end of 1996.
Growing financial costs, including debt-servicing expenses, have been blamed for the company's expanded net loss in 1996 despite a rise in total sales.
Its sales rose to 1.37 trillion in 1996 from 986.75 billion won in 1995.
